newsitem.title: MONACO: Monaco PM urges cooperation on money laundering.
newsitem.headline: Monaco PM urges cooperation on money laundering.

text.p: Monaco's outgoing prime minister Paul Dijoud on Monday urged greater cooperation with France, the United States and Italy in cracking down on money laundering.

Dijoud, 58, said he had worked hard during his two and a half years in office setting up measures to prevent money laundering in the tiny principality, a tax free banking centre on the French Riviera.

"The government of Monaco didn't go about this with half measures," Dijoud told a news conference, detailing his record under Prince Rainier on issues ranging from cracking down on crime to promoting social welfare.

Dijoud is to return to France to take up a job organising a trip by French President Jacques Chirac to Latin America in March. Prince Rainier of Monaco will pick a new premier, or Minister of State, from three candidates proposed by France.
Dijoud said that cooperation with the United States, Italy and France should be reinforced to prevent money laundering in Monaco, which is celebrating its 700th birthday this year.
Dijoud stressed the importance of Monaco as a financial centre, offering "physical security, confidentiality and political stability to those who invest with us."

He said the Monaco had set up a specialised group of experts to tackle the problem of money laundering and had expelled about 50 people thought to pose a threat to the principality, including some suspected of links to international crime.

Dijoud also said the government had taken measures to outlaw deposits of large amounts of cash in banks and to tighten rules on management of the casino, run by Monaco's biggest company, the Societe des Bains de Mer (SBM).
He said "the problem of the moral health of the casino" was "largely solved". But he said that "a casino is not a cathedral" and that continued vigilance was needed.

Described by British writer Somerset Maugham as "the sunny place for shady people", tax-free Monaco is feared to be vulnerable to money laundering given its proximity to Italian organised crime, its banking secrecy rules and economic growth.
